title: Phone Photography Tips: Focus, Exposure, Lenses and Modes — cv.cm
description: Phone photography tips for iPhone and Android: clean lens, grid, tap to focus, exposure slider, AE/AF lock, which lens to use, night mode, HDR, burst and RAW.
h1: How do you take better photos with your phone?
answer: Wipe the lens, turn on grid lines, and tap your subject to set focus and exposure, then drag the exposure slider down a little if bright areas look white. Use the 1x main camera in dim light, switch to 2x or 3x only when there is plenty of light, never pinch past the real lenses, and hold still while night mode finishes.

sections.h: What the phone decides for you
body: A phone camera has a small sensor and a fixed aperture, so it cannot change depth of field or gather light the way a large camera can. It makes up for that with processing. Each time you press the shutter, it usually captures several frames and merges them to reduce noise and keep detail in both bright and dark areas. It also guesses focus, exposure and white balance.

Most of the time those guesses are good. Your job is to give the phone good light and a steady shot, and to correct it when it guesses wrong: when it focuses on the background, when the sky turns white, or when a dark scene looks grey. The habits below fix those cases on any modern phone.

sections.h: Ten habits before you press the shutter

ol: Clean the lens. Phones live in pockets, and a greasy lens gives soft, foggy photos and glowing halos around lights. Wipe it with a soft cloth or the inside of a cotton shirt.
Turn on grid lines. On iPhone go to Settings, Camera, Grid; on Android look in camera settings. Use the lines to keep horizons level and to place the subject off centre.
Turn on the level if your phone has one. iPhone shows a level with the grid; Pixel shows framing hints that line up when the phone is straight.
Tap the subject. The tap sets both focus and exposure for that spot.
Adjust brightness. After tapping, drag the sun icon (iPhone) or the brightness slider (Android) down to keep a bright sky or white dress from turning pure white, or up to lift a dark face.
Lock it. Touch and hold the subject until AE/AF Lock (or a similar label) appears. Focus and exposure then stay fixed while you recompose or take several frames.
Hold the phone with two hands and elbows against your body. Press the shutter gently, or use a volume button.
Get closer instead of zooming. Walking two steps forward gives more detail than any digital zoom.
Check the background and the edges of the frame before you shoot.
Take a few frames. Storage is cheap; delete the extras later.

sections.h: Which lens to use: 0.5x, 1x, 2x, 3x and beyond
body: Most phones have several cameras behind the zoom buttons. They are different lenses with different sensors, not one lens that zooms. The 1x main camera almost always has the largest sensor and the widest aperture, so it gives the best quality, especially in low light.

body: A rule that works: if the light is good, choose the lens that frames the subject. If the light is poor, use 1x and crop later. For portraits, step back and use 2x or 3x; the face shape is more natural than at 1x close up. See the focal length guide for why.

sections.h: Modes: portrait, night, HDR, burst and RAW

ul: Portrait mode: blurs the background using depth information. It works best 0.5 to 2.5 m from the subject in good light. The phone tells you when you are too close, too far, or when it is too dark. Check edges around hair and glasses, and reduce the blur level if it looks cut out. Many phones let you change the blur after the photo is taken.

Night mode: turns on automatically in low light on most phones and captures for one to several seconds. Hold still until it finishes; if crosshairs appear on iPhone, line them up. Rest the phone on something solid for longer captures. On Pixel this is Night Sight.
HDR: combines bright and dark exposures so you keep sky detail and shadow detail. It is on by default on most phones. If a scene with moving people shows ghosting, take another frame.
Burst: hold or slide the shutter to take many frames per second. Use it for children, pets, sport and jumping shots, then keep the best.
Live or motion photos: record a short clip around the photo. Useful for choosing a better moment later, or for long-exposure effects such as smooth water on some phones.

RAW or ProRAW: available on some phones in settings or a Pro mode. The files keep more data for editing white balance and highlights but are several times larger. Use it for landscapes and difficult light, not for every photo.
Pro or manual mode: some phones let you set ISO, shutter speed and focus. Useful for light trails or stars on a tripod; see the night photography guide.

sections.h: Light and composition on a phone
body: Good light matters more than the phone. Shoot with the light coming from the side or from behind you, not straight into a bright sky, unless you want a silhouette. Early morning and late afternoon light is softer and warmer than midday light. Indoors, move the subject near a window.

ul: Place the subject on a grid line, not in the centre, unless the scene is symmetrical.
Look for a foreground, such as flowers, a railing or a doorway, to add depth.
Lower the phone. Shooting from waist height or ground level makes ordinary scenes look different.
Use the 4:3 ratio for the full sensor area and crop later; 16:9 and 1:1 crop the sensor in camera on many phones.
Turn the flash off for most scenes. Use it only for a close subject in the dark, or as fill in bright backlight.

body: If you want to practise the camera side of this, cv.cm's portrait camera simulator includes a phone lens (26 mm equivalent, fixed f/1.8) next to camera lenses, so you can compare how blur and distance behave.
The built-in photo editor is enough for most photos. Work in this order, and keep each change small.

ol: Crop and straighten. Fix tilted horizons and remove distractions at the edges.
Exposure or brightness. Make the subject look right first.
Highlights down and shadows up, if the sky is too bright or faces are too dark.
White balance (warmth). Make whites look white unless you want a warm or cool mood.
Saturation or vibrance. A small increase is enough; skin turns orange quickly.
Sharpness and noise reduction last, and only a little.

body: Phone edits are usually non-destructive, so you can revert to the original. For sharing, cv.cm's crop tool cuts photos to 1:1, 4:5 or 16:9, and the resize tool makes smaller files for email or the web.

body.note: Phone photos store the date, the phone model and often your GPS location. Before posting photos taken at home, check the location setting or remove it; cv.cm's exif tool shows and strips this data in the browser.

faq.q: Why do my phone photos look worse than what I see?
faq.a: Your eyes handle bright and dark areas at once, and the phone has to choose. Tap the important part, adjust exposure, and make sure HDR is on. Also clean the lens, which fixes many soft photos.

faq.q: Is it better to zoom or crop on a phone?
faq.a: Use the real lenses (for example 2x or 3x) when there is plenty of light. Beyond the longest real lens, zooming and cropping give about the same quality, so shoot wider and crop later, which also lets you change the framing.

faq.q: Should I shoot in RAW on my phone?
faq.a: Only when you plan to edit, for example a sunset, a high-contrast scene or mixed light. RAW files are much larger and look flatter before editing. For everyday photos, the normal format with the phone's processing looks better with no work.

faq.q: How do I get a blurred background on a phone?
faq.a: Use portrait mode, keep the subject 0.5 to 2.5 m away, and put the background far behind them. Without portrait mode, get close to a small subject with the 1x lens and keep the background distant.

faq.q: Do I need a tripod for phone photography?
faq.a: Not for daylight. A small phone tripod or clamp helps for night mode, light trails, group shots with a timer and self-portraits. Resting the phone on a wall or a bag also works.
